extracted.intended_audience: small business owners, PR writers, communications professionals preparing press releases for media/journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and formatting press releases that follow Associated Press (AP) style and best distribution practices for journalists and digital discovery. Covers structure, style rules, digital/mobile considerations, and distribution timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow AP style for press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: AP style — short for Associated Press style — is a standardized set of rules for grammar, punctuation, spelling, capitalization, and language usage. For press releases intended for media distribution, you should follow AP style as closely as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AP style reduces editing burden for journalists and improves pickup chances. Acceptable to keep a few consistent company-specific preferences if applied consistently. If you don't have the AP Stylebook, consult Purdue OWL or current online cheat sheets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverted pyramid structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the most important information at the beginning of the press release, with supporting details following in descending order of importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First paragraph should answer who, what, when, where, why. Ensures journalists capture essential news value even if they read only the first few paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Header elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Top-of-release elements journalists expect: centered business logo, release timing indicator, and media contact information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center your business logo at the very top. Place “FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE” in all caps on the left side (or 'EMBARGOED FOR RELEASE UNTIL [DATE AND TIME]' if applicable). Include contact information (name, phone, email) for your media contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline and subheadline best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines should be concise, attention-grabbing, and follow AP style; subheads provide additional context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use title case for headlines (see capitalization rules). Aim for headlines under 80 characters for digital distribution. Include a subheadline (dek) if necessary. Balance SEO keywords with natural language that follows AP style. Keep headline and subheadline under 80 characters combined; avoid end punctuation unless necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: AP-style headline capitalization (title case guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: AP style uses title case for press release headlines: capitalize the first word, the last word and all major words in between.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize articles (a, an, the), short conjunctions (and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet), or short prepositions (in, on, at, by, to, up, as, of, off) unless they are first or last words. Always capitalize verbs (including short ones), nouns, pronouns, adjectives, and adverbs. Examples provided for correct/incorrect capitalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: AP headline words that are not capitalized / always capitalized
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists of word classes to never capitalize (unless first/last) and to always capitalize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not capitalized: articles, short conjunctions, short prepositions. Always capitalized: verbs (Is, Are, Be, Do, Go), nouns/pronouns (He, She, It), adjectives/adverbs (New, Fast). Use examples to check correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subheadline (dek) capitalization and length
rubrics_metrics.description: Subheadlines follow same title case rules and should be concise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep headline and subheadline under 80 characters combined for optimal digital display. Avoid punctuation at the end of headlines/subheads unless a question or exclamation is necessary (best practice: use neither).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline format
rubrics_metrics.description: Dateline is the city name, in all caps, that opens the first paragraph and is separated from the body by a long dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use all caps for the city name (CHICAGO —). Add the state abbreviation if the city isn’t on AP’s standalone list (PORTLAND, Ore. —). Separate dateline from text with a long dash and spaces on both sides. Include the date only when it adds meaningful context.

rubrics_metrics.name: AP standalone dateline cities
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific list of U.S. cities that do not require a state name in datelines (AP-recognized standalone cities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page lists 29 U.S. cities plus Washington (D.C.) that stand alone (e.g., Atlanta, Boston, Chicago, New York, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Miami, Seattle, etc.). Any city not on that list must include the abbreviated state name.

rubrics_metrics.name: State abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use AP-style state abbreviations, not USPS two-letter postal codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Oregon = Ore., California = Calif., Massachusetts = Mass. Some states are never abbreviated in AP style (e.g., Texas). Refer to AP state abbreviation table for full list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead paragraph rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening paragraph must answer who, what, when, where, and why and be tightly written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep it under 35 words if possible. Lead with the news (not background). Avoid starting with phrases like 'Today, the company announced…' or burying the news behind the company name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body content organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange the remainder of the release following the inverted pyramid and readability best practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep paragraphs short (2–3 sentences). Use transition words for flow. Aim for 400–500 words total (one page) unless additional information is truly necessary; if so, place extra details in 'Notes to Editors' or linked press kit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote formatting and attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: How to include and attribute quotes in an AP-style release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always attribute quotes to specific individuals with full names and titles on first reference. Use 'said' in past tense (not 'says', 'stated', etc.). Put the attribution after the quote. Use only one attribution per quote. Prefer one quote per release (maximum two) and ensure quotes add perspective rather than restating facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate (About) section
rubrics_metrics.description: A short company description placed at the end of the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title it 'About [Company Name]'. Keep it under 100 words. Include founding date, mission, key achievements, and website URL. Write in third person and use the same boilerplate consistently across releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Include clear media contact details at the bottom of the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label 'Media Contact:' followed by the contact person’s full name, title, phone number with area code, email address, and company website.

rubrics_metrics.name: End mark to signal completion
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a standard end mark to show the release is complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditionally use ###, -END- or -30- centered on its own line. Omitting it can look amateurish and may make journalists think content was cut off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number usage rules
rubrics_metrics.description: AP rules for when to spell out numbers and when to use figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out one through nine; use figures for 10 and above. Always use figures (regardless of size) for ages, percentages (use % symbol), dimensions, temperatures, speeds, monetary amounts, addresses, and statistical data. Examples included (e.g., 'five-year-old company employs 12 people').

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentage format
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the percent symbol (%) in most cases per updated AP guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use % in all cases except at the start of a sentence. Example: 'Sales increased 14% year over year.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Date formatting rules
rubrics_metrics.description: How to write months and dates according to AP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use ordinal indicators (1st, 2nd). Abbreviate months that are six or more letters when used with a specific date (Jan., Feb., Aug., Sept., Oct., Nov., Dec.). March, April, May, June, and July are never abbreviated. When writing month and year without a date, spell out the month (e.g., 'September 2024').

rubrics_metrics.name: Job title capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for capitalizing job titles in relation to a person’s name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize titles only when they directly precede a full name (e.g., 'Chief Executive Officer Jane Smith announced…'). Lowercase when the title follows the name or stands alone ('Jane Smith, chief executive officer,' or 'the chief executive officer said…').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fancy attribution verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: AP style prefers simple past 'said' for quote attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'said' rather than 'says', 'stated', 'noted', 'explained', or 'exclaimed' — 'said' is effectively invisible to readers and reduces distraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oxford comma policy
rubrics_metrics.description: AP style generally omits the serial (Oxford) comma unless needed for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit the comma before 'and' or 'or' in lists, except when its absence would create ambiguity (then include it). Example contrasts provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid starting lead with company name
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not open the dateline-style release by leading with the company name; lead with the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of 'CHICAGO — Acme Corp. today announced…' write a lead that emphasizes the event or news and attribute appropriately in subsequent sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Boilerplate should be written in third person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid first-person language like 'We are…' because journalists may lift boilerplate verbatim; third-person reads as standard news copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: AP style for digital press releases — SEO balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate SEO strategically while maintaining AP style standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place primary keywords in the headline and first paragraph; use secondary keywords naturally in subsequent paragraphs. Avoid keyword stuffing. Consider keywords in subheadings. Examples provided showing AP-only vs AP+SEO versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperlink guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: How to use hyperlinks in digital press releases in an AP-friendly way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperlink text should make sense out of context. Don’t hyperlink entire paragraphs. Avoid 'click here'. Don’t hyperlink the company name in the boilerplate. When sharing raw URLs, include the http:// or https:// prefix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Email distribution formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Best practices for distributing releases by email.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the release in the body of the email (not just attachment). Use plain text or limited HTML. Create a subject line that includes your company name and avoid all caps or excessive punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia element guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: How to include images, captions, credits, and other assets for media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide captions for images following AP style (brief, factual descriptions). Include photo credits. Don’t embed videos directly in email releases — provide links. Offer a downloadable press kit with high-resolution images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobile optimization — text formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust text structure for readability on mobile devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit paragraphs to 2–3 sentences. Use bulleted lists for key points. Add brief subheadings to break up text. Increase white space between elements to improve scannability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobile optimization — technical considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical steps to ensure mobile-friendly delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use responsive email templates, keep attached images under 1MB, provide a plain text alternative, ensure hyperlinks have enough tappable space to avoid mis-taps, and preview on multiple devices and email clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobile multimedia specs and testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific guidance for images, videos, infographics for mobile audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optimize images to display properly on mobile (800px width maximum suggested). Include AP-style descriptions as alt text. Provide video links to mobile-friendly platforms instead of embedding. Create mobile-specific infographic versions with larger text. Test download speed for attachments on typical mobile connections and test across devices/email clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: SEO-specific optimizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactics to improve discovery while keeping AP style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary keyword in headline and first paragraph; use industry terms recognizable to journalists and searchers; include at least one internal link to a related resource; add alt text to images; avoid keyword stuffing; update evergreen content when guidance changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine newsworthiness and audience first
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing, decide whether the news merits a press release and who the target audience is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether a journalist would care if they heard the news from someone other than the company. If not newsworthy, consider a blog post or social update. Identify target audience (trade vs general business press) as framing differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose one angle and write the release around it
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus the release on a single clear news angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid announcing multiple unrelated items in one release as it dilutes news value and SEO focus. Write headline last after the body when angle is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and voice for modern press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended word count and stylistic voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep releases to 400–600 words (page also cites 400–500 words in one place). Use active voice; passive constructions are slower and more likely to be rewritten by journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution timing and follow-up etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: Best days/times and follow-up practices for sending releases to journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send on Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. in the target journalist’s time zone. Avoid Mondays and Fridays and sending after 3 p.m. Use embargoes only when necessary (set and honor exact lift times). Follow up once, 48–72 hours after distribution; multiple follow-ups harm relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of company-specific styling for trade names/product names
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect official company or product stylings even if they break AP conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep trade names like iPhone, WordPress, YouTube as styled by the company. If a product name starts with a lowercase letter and would start a sentence, rewrite to avoid capitalizing it incorrectly (e.g., 'Users of iPhone' instead of 'IPhone users').

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial figures formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: How to present monetary amounts and related numeric financial information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use figures and the $ sign for dollars (e.g., '$5', '$5.25', '$5 million'). Spell out 'cents' for amounts under a dollar (e.g., '50 cents'). Use decimals only when cents are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis communication tone and attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: AP-style application in crisis or incident press releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize straightforward factual information, minimize marketing language, and clearly identify who is making statements about the crisis. Attribution is particularly important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acronym usage
rubrics_metrics.description: How to introduce and use acronyms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out acronyms on first reference followed by the acronym in parentheses, then use the acronym subsequently. Widely recognized acronyms (FBI, NASA, CEO) do not need to be spelled out. Industry-specific acronyms should be spelled out on first reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common AP style mistakes to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Ten frequent errors spotted by journalists and how to correct them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: mistaken percent wording (use %), ordinal indicators with dates (don’t use '1st'), capitalizing job titles incorrectly, using 'says' vs 'said', incorrect number usage, misusing Oxford comma, wrong state abbreviations, starting lead with company name, boilerplate in first person, and forgetting the end mark. Use the page's examples to fix these mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work with professional editors for AP compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a distribution/editing service to ensure AP-style compliance can improve pickup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: eReleases offers editors who review releases for AP compliance and can make minor corrections automatically or work with you on major revisions. Professional distribution services can target relevant journalists, syndicate to major news sites, and provide reporting on engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicting headline-capitalization guidance (note)
rubrics_metrics.description: The page contains two different statements about headline capitalization: one saying AP uses title case, another saying AP headlines capitalize only the first word and proper nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware the guide contains inconsistent guidance; when in doubt consult the current AP Stylebook. The page provides examples for both approaches — reconcile by following the AP Stylebook edition you or your target media use.
